Best For: Next.js apps (best integration), frontend hosting (React, Vue, etc.), serverless functions, edge functions, preview deployments, automatic CI/CD (Git integration), environment variables, analytics, speed insights. Best-in-class for Next.js deployment.
Tradeoffs: Optimized for Next.js — best experience if you're using Next.js. Good for frontend + serverless functions. For separate backend (long-running server), Vercel is not ideal (use Railway/Render/Fly.io for the backend). vendor lock-in (Vercel-specific features). Pricing scales with usage (bandwidth, serverless execution, etc.).
Cost Model: Hobby: free (personal projects). Pro: $20/month (per member, includes bandwidth, serverless execution, etc.). Add-ons (analytics, etc.) extra. Enterprise: custom pricing. Usage-based beyond plan limits.
Default For: Default for Next.js full-stack apps — frontend + API routes/Server Actions + serverless functions on Vercel.

Best For: Frontend hosting (React, Vue, etc.), serverless functions, edge functions, preview deployments, automatic CI/CD (Git integration), form handling, environment variables. Good alternative to Vercel for frontend hosting.
Tradeoffs: Good frontend hosting, similar to Vercel. Not as deeply integrated with Next.js as Vercel (but supports Next.js). For separate backend (long-running server), Netlify is not ideal (use Railway/Render/Fly.io).
Cost Model: Starter: free. Pro: $19/month (per member). Enterprise: custom. Usage-based beyond plan limits.
Default For: Alternative frontend hosting — good if you prefer Netlify or have non-Next.js frontend.

Best For: Deploy backend services (Node.js, Python, Go, Rust, etc.), databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, etc.), background workers, cron jobs. Simple deployment (Git integration, Docker), good developer experience, predictable pricing. Good for separate backends that need a long-running server.
Tradeoffs: Not specifically optimized for frontend hosting (use Vercel/Netlify for frontend). For full-stack apps, pair with Vercel/Netlify for frontend + Railway for backend + database. Pricing is usage-based (compute + database), can scale with usage.
Cost Model: Usage-based: pay for what you use (compute hours, database storage, etc.). Starter: $5/month credit. Then pay as you grow. Predictable for small/medium apps, scales with usage.
Default For: Default for separate backend hosting — pair with Vercel/Netlify for frontend, Railway for backend + database.

Best For: Deploy backend services (Node.js, Python, Go, Rust, etc.), databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, etc.), background workers, cron jobs, static sites. Simple deployment (Git integration, Docker), good developer experience, predictable pricing. Good alternative to Railway.
Tradeoffs: Similar to Railway — good for backend + database hosting. Not optimized for frontend hosting (use Vercel/Netlify). Slightly different pricing/model than Railway — compare based on your needs.
Cost Model: Free tier for some services (limited). Paid: starts around $7/month for web services, database pricing separate. Usage-based for some resources. Predictable for small/medium apps.
Default For: Alternative to Railway for backend + database hosting — compare based on your needs.

Best For: Deploy backend services, databases (PostgreSQL, Redis, etc.), close to users (deploy to regions close to your audience), Docker-based deployment, good for apps that need low latency globally. More control than PaaS (you get a VM, not just a platform).
Tradeoffs: More complex than Railway/Render — you manage more (VM, networking). More control, more responsibility. Not optimized for frontend hosting (use Vercel/Netlify). Pricing can be less predictable (based on VM size, regions, bandwidth).
Cost Model: Usage-based: pay for VMs (by size + regions), bandwidth, storage. Can be cost-effective for global apps (deploy close to users). Compare based on your needs.
Default For: When you need global low-latency deployment, more control than a PaaS, or specific infrastructure needs.

Best For: Everything — EC2 (servers), RDS (managed databases), Lambda (serverless), API Gateway, S3 (storage), CloudFront (CDN), and hundreds more services. Maximum flexibility, maximum control, maximum complexity.
Tradeoffs: Maximum flexibility and control, but maximum complexity. Overwhelming for simple apps. You manage more (or use managed services). Pricing can be complex and hard to predict. Great for large-scale apps, complex infrastructure needs, or when you need specific AWS services.
Cost Model: Pay-as-you-go for almost everything (compute, storage, database, bandwidth, etc.). Can be very cheap for small apps, very expensive for large/complex apps. Hard to predict costs. Free tier available (12 months for some services).
Default For: When you need full cloud infrastructure control, large-scale apps, complex infrastructure, or specific AWS services. Overkill for simple apps — use simpler platforms (Vercel, Railway, etc.) unless you need AWS specifically.

Best For: Managed PostgreSQL database, authentication, file storage, real-time subscriptions, edge functions, auto-generated APIs (REST + GraphQL via PostgREST), row-level security, generous free tier, good DX. All-in-one backend for simple apps.
Tradeoffs: BaaS — you're tied to Supabase's features and limits. Less control than a separate backend. Security depends on RLS configuration. Vendor lock-in concerns (though data is standard PostgreSQL — you can migrate the data, but you lose managed features). Not ideal for complex backend logic that doesn't fit Supabase's model.
Cost Model: Free tier: generous (500MB database, 50k MAU auth, 1GB storage, etc.). Pro: $25/month (500k MAU auth, 8GB database, etc.). Then usage-based. Affordable for small-to-medium apps.
Default For: When you want auth + database + storage + realtime in one managed service, simple apps, prototypes, or apps where the BaaS covers your needs.

Best For: Serverless PostgreSQL — scales to zero (pay when you use it), branching (like Git for your database — create branches for development, testing, migrations), good DX, Postgres-compatible, separates storage and compute (scales independently).
Tradeoffs: Serverless PostgreSQL — not a full BaaS (no built-in auth, storage, realtime like Supabase). Just the database. Pair with other services for auth, storage, etc. Cold starts possible (but Neon optimizes this). Branching is a powerful feature for development workflows.
Cost Model: Free tier: generous (0.5 GB storage, limited compute hours). Paid: usage-based (compute hours, storage). Scales to zero — pay when you use it. Cost-effective for sporadic/low-traffic apps.
Default For: Serverless PostgreSQL for separate-backend apps — pair with your backend hosting (Railway, Render, etc.) and frontend hosting (Vercel, Netlify).

Best For: Firestore (NoSQL database), Realtime Database, authentication, hosting, cloud functions (serverless), storage, analytics, and more. All managed by Google. Good for mobile-first apps, real-time apps, quick prototypes.
Tradeoffs: NoSQL (Firestore), not SQL — tradeoffs (no joins, limited querying, eventual consistency). Vendor lock-in (Google/Firebase). Pricing can be unpredictable (pay per read/write on Firestore). Best for mobile-first, real-time, or apps already in the Firebase ecosystem.
Cost Model: Free tier: generous (Firestore: 1GB storage, 50k reads/day, etc.). Blaze plan: pay-as-you-go beyond free limits. Can be affordable for small apps, expensive at scale (especially Firestore reads/writes).
Default For: When mobile-first, real-time needs, or you're already in the Firebase ecosystem. Not the default for structured relational data — use PostgreSQL instead.
